Bread of Life
brĕd ŭv līf
n. / title (Christ as the sustenance of the soul; rendering Greek ho artos tes zoes)
Bread, Old English bread; the Greek artos is the ordinary loaf. The title takes the plainest and most necessary food in the ancient world and makes it a name for a Person.

See also: Bread of Life

Biblical Definition

Christ's self-designation in John 6: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst” (John 6:35); “I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead” (John 6:48–49); “I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world” (John 6:51). The discourse stands on the manna — “he gave them bread from heaven to eat” (John 6:31) — and on the feeding of the five thousand, and it ends with most of the crowd walking away (John 6:66).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bread as food made of flour or meal; and, in Scripture, food in general, support of life, and spiritually the doctrine of the gospel and Christ Himself.

expand to see more

BREAD, n. A mass of dough, made by moistening and kneading the flour or meal of some species of grain, and baked in an oven.

2. Food in general.

3. Support of life in general; maintenance.

BREAD OF LIFE, in a spiritual sense, Christ, the author and support of spiritual life.

Key Scripture

John 6:35 — "And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst."

John 6:48 — "I am that bread of life."

John 6:51 — "I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world."

John 6:53 — "Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you."

John 6:66 — "From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him."

John 6:31 — "Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat."

Modern Corruption

The bread of life is read as the Supper, and the discourse was preached a year before the Supper existed.

expand to see more

John 6 is the passage on which the doctrine of the mass has most often been rested, and the chronology is against the reading. The discourse is preached in a synagogue at Capernaum, at passover time, a full year before the upper room; the crowd who heard it had no ordinance to refer it to, and could not have understood it of a rite that did not exist. The Lord Himself supplies the key at the end of the chapter, when the saying proves hard: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63). The eating is believing, and He says so plainly in verse 35, where coming and believing stand in the two halves of one sentence.

That does not make the language mild. “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (John 6:53) is deliberately offensive to a people forbidden blood, and it emptied the room: from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. The Lord did not soften it or call them back; He turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away. A gospel arranged so that nobody ever walks away is not the gospel of John 6.

The manna is the argument's hinge and the corruption most often misses it. Your fathers did eat manna, and are dead — the miracle bread of the exodus, given daily for forty years, kept a nation alive and buried every one of them. What the crowd wanted was more of that: bread that solves today. Christ offers bread that solves death, and the difference between the two requests is the difference between the multitude who followed for the loaves and the disciple who says, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek artos (G740), bread, a loaf; zoe (G2222), life; trogo (G5176), to eat, chew; manna (G3131); Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread, food.

expand to see more

Greek ho artos tes zoes (G740, G2222) — the bread of life; John 6:35, 6:48; ho artos ho zon, the living bread, John 6:51.

Greek trogo (G5176) — to eat, chew; John 6:54, 6:56–58, the deliberately physical verb.

Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; Exodus 16:15, 16:31, Numbers 11:7, Joshua 5:12.

Usage

"“He that cometh to me shall never hunger” — coming and believing in one sentence."

"“Your fathers did eat manna… and are dead” — bread that solves today against bread that solves death."

"“From that time many of his disciples went back” — the sermon that emptied the room."
